activities.title: Home Magnet Survey: which magnet reaches furthest?
activities.context: In this activity you find magnets in your home and test how far each one reaches. You rank them by a fair test, and compare your ranking with your guess.

materials.item: up to 5 magnets from around the home, such as fridge magnets, a cupboard door catch, a pencil box clasp, a school bar magnet and a toy magnet (3 is enough if you cannot find 5)
a steel paper clip and a spare
a smooth table and a 30 centimetre ruler
a pencil and the results table on paper

activities.safety: Do not take anything apart to get a magnet out. Small strong magnets can pinch fingers and are dangerous if swallowed, so keep them away from little children and from your mouth. Keep magnets away from phones and watches. Ask a grown-up before borrowing a magnet from a cupboard or a bag.

schedule.what: Find five magnets, guess a ranking, measure the reach of each three times, find the means and compare.

activities.record: Make a table with the magnet, your guess for its rank, three readings and the mean. Number the magnets from furthest reach to shortest.

flow.do: 1. Walk round the home with a grown-up. 2. Find five magnets that can be taken out or lifted off. 3. Lay them on the table. 4. Write down what each one is.
flow.say: Let's find five magnets in the house. Look for a fridge magnet, a cupboard catch, a clasp and others. Which do you think reaches furthest?
flow.kid: Find five magnets. Lay them out. Guess which reaches furthest.

ask.q: Which magnet do you think reaches furthest? Why?
good: The biggest one.
The school magnet, because it is made to be strong.
The tiny one, because it looks strong.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Flat fridge magnets are weak and have stripes of poles. A cupboard door catch can be quite strong for its size. Do not use a phone, a speaker or anything with a screen. If you cannot find five, borrow from a neighbour or relative, or use three.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Home Magnet Survey. You find five magnets and guess which reaches furthest.

flow.do: 1. Lay the ruler on the table with the clip on the 0 line. 2. Slide the first magnet slowly towards the clip from about 6 centimetres (a weak fridge magnet needs to start at 3 centimetres and go in half-centimetre steps). 3. Stop when the clip moves. 4. Read the gap. 5. Do it three times. 6. Repeat for each magnet.
flow.say: Slide each magnet at the same slow speed. Stop the moment the clip moves. Write the gap three times for each magnet.
flow.kid: Test each magnet three times. Write the gap each time.
flow.parent: Always use the same face of each magnet. For a flat fridge magnet, use the flat side. For a catch, use the end that touches the cupboard. Do not bring phones near the magnets. Fridge magnets and flat catches are weak, so their reach may be under 1 centimetre. Always show the same face to the clip and use a fresh clip each time. With 2 to 4 children, each brings one or two magnets and each child tests a magnet that is not theirs: one slides, one reads the gap, one writes.
flow.context: In this step, you measure the reach of each magnet three times.

flow.do: Work out the mean for each magnet. Rank them. Compare with your guess.
flow.say: Find the mean for each magnet. Which reached furthest? Did that match your guess?
flow.kid: Find each mean. Rank the magnets. Was your guess right?

check.q: One magnet's three readings were 3.0, 3.2 and 6.0 centimetres. What is the best thing to do?
options: Use only the 6.0, because it is the biggest
Test that magnet again, because 6.0 does not fit the other two
Ignore that magnet
check.why: A reading far from the others may be a slip, such as moving the magnet too fast. Test again and see if it repeats. Throwing it away without checking would hide what really happened.

flow.context: In this step, you find the mean for each magnet and compare with your guess.
flow.parent: Does a bigger magnet always reach further? Check the sizes against the ranking. Typical readings are under 1 centimetre for fridge magnets and 2 to 4 centimetres for a school bar magnet.

setup.caption: 1. Lay out your five magnets. Guess which reaches furthest.

setup.art: A ruler on a smooth table with a clip at the 0 line and a fridge magnet being slid towards it.
setup.caption: 2. Test each magnet three times with the clip and ruler.

projects.title: The Ghost Maze: a clip that follows a hidden magnet
projects.context: In this 2-day project you build a maze on a thin board and make a paper clip run through it, led by a magnet you hold underneath. You find the thickest board your magnet can lead a clip through.

materials.item: a shoebox lid or a piece of stiff card about the size of a shoebox lid
6 or more strips of thin card about 1 centimetre wide, cut from a cereal box
glue or sticky tape
a steel paper clip (it may flip over; a small steel nut or washer slides better but needs a closer magnet), as the ghost
a bar magnet
2 stacks of books to rest the board on, each about 8 centimetres high

about 10 pieces of cardboard from cartons (each about 3 millimetres thick and about 8 centimetres square), or 6 to 8 thin exercise notebooks, to test thickness; a school magnet typically leads a clip through only about 1 to 3 centimetres of card
a ruler and a pencil

schedule.what: Plan a maze on paper and build it on the lid with card strips. Rest the lid on two stacks of books.
Lead the clip through the maze. Add layers of card under the maze to find the thickest board the magnet can lead through.

projects.record: Draw your maze. Write how many layers of card the magnet led the clip through and the total thickness, including the lid. Compare it with the reach you measured in the Add or Cancel test.

flow.do: 1. Draw a maze on paper, with a start and an end. 2. Make the walls from card strips, glued to the lid. 3. Leave paths about 3 centimetres wide. 4. Let the glue dry.
flow.say: Plan the maze first. Make the paths wide enough for a clip to move along. Which walls will make it hard?
flow.kid: Draw a maze. Glue card walls to the lid. Make the paths wide.
flow.parent: Keep the maze simple. Four or five walls are enough. The glue needs time to dry, so you may prefer tape. Plain glue takes hours to dry, so tape the walls for a quick start or build on Day 1 and test on Day 2. With 2 to 4 children, each builds a small maze on their own lid, or all build one big one, then swap and lead each other's clip: one leads, one times the run with a phone, one watches the clip. One magnet and one clip can be shared.
flow.context: This is the first day of the Ghost Maze. You plan the maze and build its walls.

flow.do: 1. Rest the lid on two stacks of books, with a gap underneath. 2. Put the clip at the start of the maze. 3. Hold the magnet under the lid, touching it. 4. Slide the magnet to lead the clip through.
flow.say: Hold the magnet under the lid, and move it. The clip follows. Can you lead it all the way through the maze?
flow.kid: Put the clip in the maze. Hold the magnet below. Lead the clip through.
flow.parent: The clip may stick on a wall if you go too fast. Move slowly. If the clip does not follow at all, check that it is steel and that the magnet is touching the lid.
flow.context: In this step, you lead the clip through the maze with a magnet you hold underneath.

flow.do: 1. Tape a piece of cardboard on the flat top of the magnet. 2. Hold the magnet with the cardboard touching the underside of the lid and try to lead the clip through the maze. 3. Tape another piece on top of the first. 4. Keep adding pieces until the clip will not follow.
flow.say: Add one sheet of card at a time between the magnet and the lid. How many sheets can the magnet lead the clip through?
flow.kid: Add card between the magnet and the lid. How many layers can it manage?
flow.parent: Count the sheets. Then measure the total thickness of all the layers with a ruler, including the lid. This is the thickness your magnet can reach through. Taping the pieces to the magnet keeps the pile together while you slide it. The cardboard of the lid counts as part of the thickness.
flow.context: This is the second day of the project. You add card layers to find the thickest board that works.

flow.do: 1. Measure the total thickness when the clip stopped following. 2. Compare it with the reach from the Add or Cancel test. 3. Try two magnets side by side, north with north, and see if they lead the clip through a thicker pile.
flow.say: Measure the pile at the point where the clip stopped. Is it close to the reach you measured in the Add or Cancel test? What happens with two magnets?
flow.kid: Measure the pile of card. Try two magnets side by side. What changes?

check.q: A magnet leads a clip through 3 centimetres of card but not 5. You tape a second magnet beside it, north to north. What is the best prediction?
options: It will now lead through about 4 centimetres
It will now lead through 6 centimetres exactly
It will lead through the same 3 centimetres, no more
check.why: Two magnets side by side with like poles together add their fields, so the reach grows. But the pull fades so fast with distance that the reach grows only a little. If you chose 6 centimetres, you assumed that twice the magnets give twice the reach.

flow.context: In this step, you measure the thickness the magnet reached through and test two magnets together.
flow.parent: Typically the thickness the clip follows through is a little less than the reach measured in Add or Cancel, because the clip must also be dragged against friction. For two magnets, hold them together with rubber bands, north with north.

flow.do: Draw your maze and write down the thickest pile your magnet could lead the clip through.
flow.say: What was the thickest pile? Why can't the magnet reach through more? What would let it?
flow.kid: Write the thickest pile. Why can't it reach through more?

ask.q: Why does the clip stop following when the pile gets too thick?
good: The pull fades with distance.
The clip is too far from the magnet's field.
The field is too weak out there.

flow.context: In this last step, you record your result and explain why the magnet has a limit.

challenges.title: The Quiet Pair: two magnets that hardly disturb a compass
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You arrange two magnets so that they disturb a compass 10 centimetres away as little as possible. A pair that hardly turns the needle is called a quiet pair.
challenges.problem: One bar magnet 10 centimetres from a compass turns the needle by a large angle. Arrange two identical magnets, using only tape, so that the needle turns by as little as possible from 10 centimetres away.
constraints: Use exactly two identical bar magnets.
The compass stays on its spot, 10 centimetres from the nearest part of the magnets.
You may use tape and nothing else, except a steel strip as a keeper if you have one.
You may not cut or break the magnets.
materials: a sheet of paper with a north line drawn on it
a steel strip, such as an old steel ruler or a long iron nail, if you have one
general: Place the two magnets side by side with a north end next to a south end. Their fields point opposite ways and partly cancel.
Measure the turn for one magnet first. That is the number to beat.
Measure the turn for your pair, and see how much smaller it is.
creative: Try laying a steel strip across both ends as a keeper. Does it make the pair quieter?
Try different arrangements, such as end to end or at an angle, and find which is quietest.
Put the pair on the other side of the compass and see if the turn changes.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own quiet pair. Draw your arrangement, test it, and record the turn. Does the quietest pair match what you expected from the field picture?

flow.do: Place the compass on its spot with the north line drawn. Put one magnet 10 centimetres away, end towards the compass. Measure how far the needle turns.
flow.say: How far does one magnet turn the needle from 10 centimetres? That is the number to beat.
flow.kid: Test one magnet at 10 centimetres. Measure the turn. That is your score to beat.

ask.q: What arrangement do you think will be quietest? Why?
good: Side by side with opposite ends together, so the fields cancel.
End to end, so the pulls cancel.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Quiet Pair challenge. You measure one magnet and guess how to do better.

flow.do: Tape the two magnets in your first arrangement. Place them 10 centimetres from the compass. Measure the turn. Change the arrangement and measure again.
flow.say: Tape the magnets in a new way. Measure the turn. Which arrangement turns the needle the least?
flow.kid: Tape the magnets. Measure the turn. Try a new arrangement.
flow.parent: Side by side with unlike poles together should turn the needle by much less than one magnet does. If the turn is big, check which ends are together. Do not hold magnets close to other magnets, as they can snap together and pinch.
flow.context: In this step, you build and test different pairs and measure the needle each time.

flow.do: Draw your quietest pair with the field lines you expect. Explain why it is quiet.
flow.say: Draw your quietest pair and draw how the field lines go. Why does the needle hardly turn?
flow.kid: Draw your quietest pair. Why does the needle hardly turn?

check.q: Two identical magnets are side by side, with a north pole next to a south pole. Why is the pair quieter than one magnet?
options: The two fields point opposite ways and partly cancel
The magnets are twice as heavy
The compass is attracted to both equally
check.why: At a distance, the field of one magnet points one way and the field of the other points the opposite way, so they largely cancel. The magnets are not weaker. Their fields work against each other. If you chose heavier, remember that weight does not change a magnetic field.

items: a tin box that sticks to a magnet

items.p: A magnet has to touch a paper clip to pull it.
items.why: False. A magnet's force acts across a gap. The clip can jump to a magnet from a few centimetres away.

items.why: True. The red end of a compass shows the direction of the field. It points away from the north pole and towards the south pole.

away

items.p: A bar magnet's pull is strongest at its ______.
a: poles
ends

Mark a dot at each end of the needle
Slide the compass so its white end sits on the last dot

items.a: Curved lines leave the north pole, loop round the outside and enter the south pole. They are closest together near the poles.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the lines bunching at the poles, where the field is strongest, and spreading out far away.

items.p: Explain why a paper clip jumps towards a magnet before it touches it.
items.a: The magnet has a magnetic field around it. When the clip is inside the field, it becomes a temporary magnet and the magnet pulls it. The force acts across the gap.
items.why: A strong answer uses the word field, and says the clip becomes a temporary magnet in it.

items.p: Explain how a small compass can show the direction of a magnet's field at a spot.
items.a: A compass needle is a small magnet that can turn freely. In a field, it turns to line up with the field. Its red end points along the field's direction.
items.why: A strong answer says the needle is a small magnet that lines up along the field.

items.p: A magnet is held 2 centimetres from a clip, with a sheet of paper between them. What happens?
opts: The clip is pulled, because paper does not block the field
The clip is not pulled, because the paper is in the way
items.why: Paper does not block a magnetic field, so the clip is pulled as if nothing were there.

items.p: You dip a bar magnet in a heap of paper clips. Where on the magnet do most of the clips cling?
opts: At the middle of the long side
items.why: The field is strongest at the poles, which are at the ends, so most clips cling there.

items.p: Three tries of a reach test gave 3, 4 and 5 centimetres. What is the mean?
items.why: Add the three readings: 3 plus 4 plus 5 is 12. Then divide by 3, which gives 4. If you chose 12, you forgot to divide.

items.p: Which of these best describes a magnetic field?
opts: A metal wire inside the magnet
The region around a magnet where its force can be felt
items.why: A field is the region around a magnet where the magnetic force acts. At every spot in it, the force has a strength and a direction.

items.p: Two friends argue about why a magnet can pull a paper clip across a gap.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with the second friend, because a magnet's force works in empty space, as the Earth's field does far above the air. It also says what the first friend has right: the field does pass through air, but the air is not what carries the force.
items.why: This question checks that the child understands that the field, and not the air, reaches across the gap.

views.says: The air carries the pull from the magnet to the clip.
Magnets work in empty space too, so the pull does not need air.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use what you know about magnets and the Earth. Then say one thing the other friend has right.

items.p: Two identical bar magnets are taped side by side with their north poles together. Compared with one magnet, the pair reaches...
items.why: The fields point the same way and add, so the pair reaches further. But the pull fades so fast with distance that the reach grows only a little.

items.p: A compass is placed at 10 centimetres and 20 centimetres from a magnet. At 10 it turns 54 degrees, and at 20 it turns 15. What does this show?
opts: The turn dropped to less than half when the distance doubled
items.why: Half of 54 is 27, and the turn at 20 centimetres was 15, which is less than half. The pull fades faster than the distance grows.

items.p: A shop stores bar magnets in a box in pairs, with the north pole of one next to the south pole of the other. Why?
opts: The fields partly cancel, so less field leaks out and the magnets stay strong
Magnets cannot touch their own kind
items.why: With unlike poles together, the two fields point opposite ways and largely cancel outside. The magnets also hold each other's domains in line.

items.p: Which of these would best protect a compass from a strong magnet nearby?
items.why: A thick iron tin takes the field into its walls, so little reaches the inside. The others let the field pass.

items.p: A magnet that picks up a clip from 3 centimetres is replaced by one that is 4 times stronger. How far will it reach?
opts: A bit more than 3 centimetres, but much less than 12
items.why: The pull fades so fast with distance that a much stronger magnet reaches only a little further.

items.p: When two fields point in opposite directions at the same spot, they partly ______.
a: cancel
items.why: Fields add as arrows do. Two arrows pointing opposite ways subtract from each other.

items.p: A thick sheet of ______ or steel can take a magnet's field into itself.
a: iron
items.why: Iron and steel are easier for the field to pass through than air, so the field gathers into them.

items.p: A single magnetic pole on its own, a north without a south, has never been found.
items.why: True. Cut a magnet in two and each piece gets two poles. Physicists have searched for a single pole and have not found one.

items.p: Field lines can cross each other.
items.why: False. At any spot, the field has just one direction, so two lines cannot cross there.

items.p: Explain why two magnets side by side can pull a clip from further away or from less far, depending on which way round one of them is.
items.a: A magnetic field has a direction at each spot, and two fields add like arrows. With like poles together the arrows point the same way and add up. With unlike poles together they point against each other and partly cancel.
items.why: A strong answer says that fields have direction, and that they add or cancel.

items.p: Describe how you could test whether a lid shields a paper clip from a magnet, and what you would see if it did.
items.a: Find a gap where the magnet just moves the clip. Put the lid between the magnet and the clip. If the clip no longer moves, the lid takes the field into itself and shields the clip.
items.why: A strong answer uses a fair test, with the same gap and only the lid changing.

items.p: Two students look at a picture of iron filings making lines around a magnet and talk about what the lines are.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with the second student, because each filing turns into a tiny magnet and lines up with the field, so the lines show direction and are not threads. It also says what the first student has right: the filings really do form lines, and the field is a real thing that makes them.
items.why: This question checks that the child can tell the lines of a drawing from the field behind them.

views.says: Invisible threads in the air hold the filings in lines.
Each filing turns to point along the field. The lines are a drawing of the direction.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Say what each student has right.

items.p: Which box would best protect a watch from a magnet outside it?

items.p: At the north pole of a bar magnet, a compass needle points straight away from the pole. In the middle of the side, it points along the magnet. What does this show?

The magnet is stronger in the middle
The compass only works at poles

items.p: Dropping a magnet many times on a hard floor can slowly make it weaker.

items.p: A friend puts a second compass beside yours while you draw a field map. Explain why that would spoil your map.

items.p: A magnet can lead a clip through 3 centimetres of card but not through 6. Explain why, using the word field.
items.a: The field of the magnet fades quickly with distance. At 6 centimetres the field at the clip is too weak to pull it, but at 3 centimetres it is strong enough.
items.why: A strong answer says the field is weaker further away, and that the card does not block it.

items.p: Two field lines can never cross. Explain why.
items.a: At any spot, the field has only one direction. A line shows that direction. If two lines crossed, the field would have two directions at the crossing spot, which is impossible.
items.why: A strong answer says that the field has one direction at each spot.

items.p: Two students talk about whether a magnetic field is a real thing in space.
items.a: A strong answer says this is still argued, and says what each student has right. The first student has the evidence that fields carry energy and make waves of light. The second student is right that we only ever measure forces on things, and that field lines are drawings.
items.why: This question checks that the child can weigh two reasonable ideas and say what is known and what is not.

views.says: The field is real. It carries energy through empty space, and it can make radio waves.

items.ask: Whose idea is better supported? What is the thing that nobody can tell for certain?

Laying a steel keeper across its poles

quiz.why: The field spreads out and bends back, so the pull fades very quickly with distance.

quiz.p: Two identical magnets are side by side, with a north pole next to a south pole. What happens to the field far away?
quiz.why: The fields point opposite ways and partly cancel outside the pair.

quiz.p: Which of these would stop a magnet from pulling a clip on the other side?
quiz.why: Iron takes the field into itself. The others let the field pass.

quiz.p: Using field lines, why do unlike poles attract and like poles repel?
opts: They come from one field, and the lines join unlike poles and bunch between like poles
Because north is stronger than south

quiz.p: Field lines drawn close together in one place show that the field there is...

quiz.p: Does a magnet's field exist in empty space, with no air at all?

quiz.p: A small magnet is moved to twice the distance from a clip. The pull on the clip becomes...
quiz.why: The pull fades much faster than the distance grows. Doubling the distance cuts the pull by much more than half.

quiz.p: Why are magnets stored in pairs with unlike poles together and a steel bar across the ends?

quiz.p: Why do scientists repeat a test three times and find the mean?

To make the test last longer
Because three is a lucky number
The mean is always the biggest reading
quiz.why: A single reading can be off by a slip. The mean of several readings is a fairer answer and shows if one reading does not fit.

open_questions.q: What is a magnetic field, really? Is it a real thing in space, or a very good way to calculate forces?
open_questions.why_open: Physicists use fields every day, and fields predict radio waves and light. But whether a field is a thing or a way of describing is still discussed by philosophers of science.

open_questions.q: Could a single magnetic pole, a north without a south, exist somewhere in the universe?
open_questions.why_open: Some theories of physics say it could. Careful searches since the 1980s have found none, but nobody can say it does not exist.

open_questions.q: How do some birds and other animals sense the Earth's magnetic field?
open_questions.why_open: There is good evidence that some birds, turtles and bacteria use this field to find their way. How birds do it is debated, and scientists are still testing ideas.

open_questions.q: Why can we shield a magnetic field with iron but never shield gravity?
open_questions.why_open: Gravity has only one kind of pull, and magnetism has two kinds of pole. Physicists have good explanations, but the deeper link between forces is still being searched for.

open_questions.q: How strong can a magnet get?
open_questions.why_open: The strongest magnetic fields in the universe are near stars called magnetars, far beyond any made on Earth. How far scientists can push magnets in the laboratory is still being explored.

open_questions.q: Can a magnet be made that is strong at room temperature and does not need rare metals?
open_questions.why_open: The strongest magnets today use rare metals that are costly and hard to mine. Materials scientists are still trying to find better ones.

maths.problem: In the Add or Cancel test, three tries for one magnet's end gave reaches of 3.5, 4.0 and 4.5 centimetres. What is the mean reach?
maths.explain: Add the three reaches: 3.5 plus 4.0 plus 4.5 is 12.0. Divide by 3. 12 divided by 3 is 4. The mean reach is 4.0 centimetres.
maths.context: In the Add or Cancel test, you slide a magnet towards a clip three times and measure the gap each time.
maths.why_maths: A test never gives exactly the same number twice, so the mean of three tries gives a fairer answer than one try.

maths.problem: A magnet's mean reach at its end was 6 centimetres and at the middle of its side was 2 centimetres. How many times as far does the end reach as the side?
maths.explain: Divide the end reach by the side reach. 6 divided by 2 is 3. The end reaches 3 times as far as the side.
maths.context: In the Add or Cancel test, you compare the reach of a magnet's end with the reach of its side.
maths.why_maths: Dividing one reach by another shows by how many times a magnet is stronger at one place than another.

maths.problem: In a compass test, the needle turned 80 degrees at 5 centimetres, 55 degrees at 10 centimetres and 15 degrees at 20 centimetres. Between which two distances did the turn drop faster for each centimetre of distance?
maths.explain: From 5 to 10 centimetres the turn dropped 25 degrees over 5 centimetres, which is 5 degrees for each centimetre. From 10 to 20 centimetres it dropped 40 degrees over 10 centimetres, which is 4 degrees for each centimetre. So the drop for each centimetre was faster between 5 and 10.
maths.context: In the Fading Pull test, you measure how far a compass needle turns at different distances from a magnet.
maths.why_maths: Comparing how steeply a line falls in different places shows where the pull of a magnet fades fastest.

maths.problem: Inside a magnet, a square of iron is shown as 20 small arrows. Sixteen of the arrows point to the right and 4 point in other directions. What fraction of the arrows point to the right? What does that suggest about the iron?
maths.answer: 4 out of 5, or four fifths. The iron is mostly lined up, so it is a magnet.
maths.explain: The fraction is 16 out of 20. Divide both numbers by 4: 16 divided by 4 is 4, and 20 divided by 4 is 5. So the fraction is 4 out of 5. Most arrows line up, so their fields add up.
maths.context: Inside a magnet, tiny regions called domains point the same way. In plain iron they point every which way.
maths.why_maths: A fraction tells us how much of the iron is lined up, and the larger it is, the stronger the magnet.

maths.problem: You place a compass at 12 spots, spaced evenly round a magnet, to map its field. A full turn is 360 degrees. How many degrees apart are neighbouring spots, measured from the middle of the magnet?
maths.explain: Twelve equal gaps share the 360 degrees. 360 divided by 12 is 30. Each neighbouring pair of spots is 30 degrees apart.
maths.context: In Walk the Compass, you place a compass at spots around a magnet to find the direction of its field.
maths.why_maths: Spacing spots evenly round a circle makes sure the map covers all sides of the magnet.

maths.problem: Four tries of a magnet's reach gave 3.0, 3.2, 6.0 and 3.1 centimetres. One reading does not fit. What should you do first, and what is the mean of the three that fit?
maths.answer: Test again to see if the odd reading repeats. The mean of the three that fit is 3.1 centimetres.
maths.explain: The 6.0 is far from the others, so it may be a slip, like moving the magnet too fast. Test again. The three that fit add to 9.3 (3.0 plus 3.2 plus 3.1). Divide by 3 to get 3.1.
maths.context: In the Home Magnet Survey, you test each magnet several times and find the mean.
maths.why_maths: Spotting a reading that does not fit helps you decide whether to trust your results or repeat the test.

maths.problem: A sheet of thin card is 0.5 millimetre thick. A magnet can lead a clip through 4 centimetres of card. How many sheets is that? Remember that 1 centimetre is 10 millimetres.
maths.explain: 4 centimetres is 40 millimetres. Each sheet is half a millimetre, so there are 2 sheets in every millimetre. 40 times 2 is 80 sheets.
maths.context: In the Ghost Maze project, you add layers of card between the magnet and the clip until it stops following.
maths.why_maths: Changing centimetres to millimetres lets you count how many thin sheets fit in the reach of a magnet.

maths.problem: A bar magnet's field pattern is drawn with lines from the north pole to the south pole. How many lines of symmetry does the pattern have?
maths.explain: One line runs along the length of the magnet through both poles. The other runs across the middle of the magnet. Folding the picture along either line makes the two halves match.
maths.context: In Walk the Compass, you draw the field lines of a bar magnet, and the pattern is the same on both sides.
maths.why_maths: Seeing the symmetry in a field map helps you check that your drawing is right, and tells you the field is balanced.

roots.context: We have drawn the invisible field around a magnet, measured how it fades and seen how two fields can add or cancel. Now we ask what that tells us about space and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In the Add or Cancel test, two magnets side by side reached further than one when their north poles were together. When one was turned round, the same pair reached much less far. The magnets had not changed, only the way their fields met. So one pull can cancel another, and what a magnet does depends on its neighbours.
deep_truth.habit: We think of a magnet as having a fixed strength, like its colour or its weight, that it carries everywhere. But the pull outside a magnet depends on the whole set-up around it, and not on the magnet alone.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Add or Cancel test, two taped magnets with north poles together reached further than one, and the same two turned north to south reached much less. If your results differ, write them down as they are and test again.

three.who_am_i: Your heart and your brain make tiny magnetic fields, many millions of times weaker than a fridge magnet's. Doctors can measure them with very sensitive detectors to see how a heart or a brain is working.
three.what_is_life: Some bacteria make a chain of tiny magnets inside their bodies and line up with the Earth's field. Scientists think this helps them find the muddy water where they live.
three.what_is_this_world: The Earth, the Sun and many stars have magnetic fields that reach far into space. The space between a magnet and a clip is not empty of force, and neither is the space between planets.

roots.thread: At the start, the magnet looked like a lump of steel, and the clip looked far away. The compass showed that the magnet is more than the lump. It has a field that reaches out and shapes the space around it. A clip, a compass or another magnet that enters the field is changed by it. Fields add and cancel, so one magnet changes what its neighbour does. What happens at any spot depends on everything nearby, and not on one magnet alone.

science.text: Every magnetic field is made by moving electric charge. Oersted found in 1820 that a current turns a compass needle, and the magnetism of a magnet comes from the spin of its electrons.
Whether a field is a real thing in space or only a very good way of calculating forces is still discussed by physicists and philosophers.

other_view.who: Some physicists and philosophers of science
other_view.view: A field is a tool for calculating. All we ever measure is the force on a clip or a compass. We can say a field fills the space, but that does not prove that something is really there.

practice.title: Feel the push in the gap
practice.say: Hold one magnet in each hand with the same poles facing. Move them slowly towards each other. Feel the push grow before they touch. Breathe in as they come closer. Breathe out as you let them move apart. Do this five times. Notice that you can feel a push where you can see nothing.
practice.kid: Hold two magnets with the same poles facing. Bring them close slowly. Feel the push. Breathe in, then out. Do it five times.

A family has not tried them at home yet, so the numbers below are typical, not promised. The reach tests need bar magnets with poles at their ends: bendy fridge magnets have stripes of poles and will not give clear results. A school bar magnet usually moves a steel clip from about 2 to 4 centimetres on a smooth table, and two taped together with like poles together reach a little further. With unlike poles together the reach is clearly smaller, but the exact numbers depend on the magnets. Each set-up is tried three times and the mean is found. For the field map, the compass needle should be small and the table must have no steel nearby, as iron bends the picture. The Fading Pull test turns the needle by about 70 to 85 degrees at 5 centimetres and by only a few degrees at 30. how_we_found_out.context: How did scientists find out that a magnet's pull is carried by something in the space around it? This card tells how a bookbinder's apprentice found out.
how_we_found_out.story: For a long time after Isaac Newton, many scientists pictured a magnet's pull as jumping straight across empty space, with nothing in between. Newton himself found this hard to believe, but his sums worked. Michael Faraday, born in 1791 to a poor family in London, was apprenticed to a bookbinder as a boy. He taught himself science from the books he bound, and he never learned much advanced maths. Faraday pictured the space around a magnet as full of lines that stretch from the north pole to the south pole. He sprinkled iron filings on paper over magnets and showed that they line up along curves. In a paper of 1852 he argued that these lines of force are real, and that the space itself carries the pull. Later, a Scottish scientist called James Clerk Maxwell turned Faraday's pictures into equations. The equations predicted waves of light and radio.
how_we_found_out.who: Michael Faraday, an English scientist (1791 to 1867), and James Clerk Maxwell, a Scottish scientist
how_we_found_out.when: Faraday's lines of force were studied from the 1830s to 1852. Maxwell's equations came in 1865.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Many scientists thought a magnet's pull jumps straight across empty space with nothing in between. Faraday argued that the space around a magnet carries lines of force, which iron filings can show.
how_we_found_out.art: A young man in a London laboratory sprinkling iron filings on a sheet of paper over a bar magnet, with curved lines of filings forming.
